plate.viewWhy: Census view is side: the arms pressing straight out from the chest (c5, c6), the back straight and tall without an arch (c5, c8) and the soft knees (c2) read from the side. The census note says the rotation fault (c7) cannot be drawn from this view.
plate.equipment: Cable column and stack with a single handle at about chest height, the cable running out to one side of the lifter (c1); floor line.
plate.start: Standing side-on to the column, feet hip-width, hips straight, knees slightly bent, chest up (c2); handle held in both hands with the fingers laced, at the chest, elbows in by the sides (c3); stepped out so the cable pulls (c4).
plate.end: Arms straight out in front of the chest at chest height, handle in line with the chest (c5, c6, c8); back straight and tall, lower back not arched (c5, c8); shoulders down, chest up (c10). Held about 2 s (c12).

mistake.what: Lower back over-arching while pressing and returning the handle.
mistake.why: LR-31 step 2: Motra lists "Over-arching lower back" among its common mistakes and its cue "Maintain neutral spine to protect back" ties the fault to harm (c8, D-SUP-PROTECT). The arch shows from the side; the rotation fault cannot be drawn (census). How often it happens is not measured.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: over-arching the lower back (c8). Common-mistakes lists read (all written for this exercise), in source order: BarBend "Common Pallof Press Mistakes": 1 Torso Twisting, 2 Not Pressing Straight, 3 Standing Too Close (or Too Far) (a set-up choice, not a candidate); Garage Gym Reviews "Common Pallof Press Exercise Mistakes": 1 Too Much Rotation, 2 Poor Pressing Position (elevated shoulders), 3 Watch Your Lower Back (overarching or flexing the lower back); Motra "Common Mistakes": 1 Allowing torso rotation, 2 Rushing the press, 3 Over-arching lower back, 4 Locking knees, 5 Leaning toward cable. ACE and StrengthLog have no list. Step 1: no frequency word counts for a fault of this exercise. Set aside: the headings "Common Pallof Press Mistakes", "Common Pallof Press Exercise Mistakes", "Common Mistakes", "Frequently Asked Questions" and "Typical Rep Range"; Garage Gym Reviews' "Here are some common mistakes to avoid when performing the Pallof press." is a list sentence; BarBend's "This is often one of the first progressions used with beginners as it’s generally easier to do." is about a variation, "The obliques are challenged isometrically to resist rotation, often responsible for shearing forces placed on the lumbar spine." about a muscle, "who often rotate to throw and catch a ball" about athletes' sports, and "The transverse abdominals (often targeted through plank variations)" about another exercise; BarBend's "it will become more and more tempting to drift them toward the side that the band is fixed on" (c6) says the drift tempts, not that many do it (read like 'tend'); its "many gymgoers don’t know how to brace properly" is about bracing in heavy lifts generally (R-LB7-3). Step 2: harm words were checked on every list item and every rotation line. Only one named fault is tied to harm: over-arching the lower back (Motra list item 3 "Over-arching lower back"), by Motra's cue "Maintain neutral spine to protect back" (c8; D-SUP-PROTECT: the cue that corrects the fault protects a named body part; Motra's range line asks to "retract to chest without arching spine"). No other fault is tied to harm, so step 2's tie order (on a list, more harm sources, direct, earlier on a list naming both, step 3's count) is not reached. Checked and set aside: Garage Gym Reviews' Watch Your Lower Back text "Overarching your lower back or putting it into flexion puts the anterior and posterior core muscles at a disadvantage, and you’ll lose all the benefits of this wonderful core exercise." (c9) states lost effect, no harm word; the rotation lines carry no harm word: BarBend's "you should avoid bending or twisting at the torso or hips at all costs, as it defeats the purpose of the exercise" (c7), Garage Gym Reviews' "if too much resistance is used, it will cause your torso to rotate, and then all the benefits of the Pallof press disappear like magic" (c7) and "The benefits of the Pallof press are lost if your torso and midsection rotates.", Motra's "Reduce weight if rotation occurs" (c7); Garage Gym Reviews' "Pressing with elevated shoulders puts the spine out of position, and the upper traps get too involved." (c10) and BarBend's "This will take tension off your trunk and make the movement easier." (c6) state no harm. Harm words that name no fault of this exercise: Motra's "Avoid if acute lower back pain present" (c19) and When to Avoid "Acute lower back injury" (conditions); Garage Gym Reviews' "If you have back pain, the Pallof press is the better choice." and "If you don’t have back pain, the Pallof press and the plank deserve a place in your workout routine." (exercise choice); BarBend's "decrease injury risks when placing heavy loads on the spine or performing loaded carries", "minimizing excessive strain on the lumbar spine is key to longevity" and "help you protect yourself from back injuries in the future" (benefits for other lifts), "Can I do the Pallof press if I have lower back pain?" (a question) and "enough muscular stress to build up your six-pack" (training stimulus). Reading not taken (D-SUP-LB9-PALLOF rules the tie above): if Motra's neutral-spine cue were not read as the cue for its arch item, no fault is tied to harm and step 3 decides by D-SUP-LB6-CCP's count, the read sources that tell the lifter to avoid each fault (sources, not lists): torso rotation 3 (BarBend, Garage Gym Reviews, Motra; c7); over-arching or flexing the lower back 2 (Garage Gym Reviews, Motra; c8, c9); not pressing straight 1 (BarBend, c6); elevated shoulders 1 (Garage Gym Reviews, c10); rushing the press, locking knees and leaning toward the cable 1 each (Motra). Lines that only give the right position are not counted (StrengthLog's "press your arms straight out in front of you without rotating your torso" and ACE's "Keep the back straight and tall", c5; Motra's "Keep hips and shoulders square"). Torso rotation would then be the top fault; the census note says the rotation fault cannot be drawn, so drawable would be false and plate.mistake would be the arch, next by the same count (2). The plate shows the arch under either reading; only handlingMistakes[0] would change. The arched lower back is a still sign the side view shows, so drawable is true.

tells.text: Hands move in a straight line

tempo.text: Up 1 and down 3 are Motra's Tempo 3-2-1 (c13, WEAK). Its Tempo tooltip gives the order eccentric (lowering), bottom pause, concentric (lifting), top pause; the page shows three numbers, read as the first three: 3 s eccentric (bringing the handle back to the chest), a 2 s bottom pause (handle at the chest, between the return and the next press) and 1 s concentric (the press out). That 2 s pause is not right after the concentric, so it is named here and not written in pause (LR-33); 3-2-1 has no fourth number, so it fixes no top pause. Pause 2 is the hold right after the press out, sourced (R-LB2-1) but from two sources with different ranges for the same phase: ACE "hold for 2-3 seconds" and Motra's own How to Perform step "Hold for 1-2 seconds resisting rotation." (c12). 2 s is the lowest (and only) value in the overlap of the two ranges (D-SUP-LB9-RANGE). StrengthLog's "Hold briefly" (c11) gives no seconds. BarBend's "5 sets of 5 reps with a very slow and controlled tempo" is a technique-learning option with no seconds.

plate.variantLine: Cable column drawn (census equipment: cable). BarBend's and Garage Gym Reviews' band set-up (anchor at chest height, step out for tension) and their form lines hold for both; Garage Gym Reviews says band and cable are interchangeable.

setup.step: Set a single handle at about chest height.
Stand side-on to the machine, feet hip-width apart.
Hold the handle in both hands at your chest, fingers laced.
Walk out until you feel the pull of the cable.

posture.point: Back straight and tall. Don't arch your lower back.
Keep your hips and shoulders square.
Press your hands in a straight line.
Breathe out as you press, in as you return.

add.why: StrengthLog and Motra list abs with the obliques as primary (c14); BarBend says the rectus abdominis contracts to stabilise the spine (c15). abs is the drawn region for the library's text-only core (content.md 8; bear_crawl, R-W0-4).

libraryDiff.why: Library: core and obliques primary, no secondary. obliques stay primary (c14). core stays in the library primary and in no feel role (LR-35). abs is proposed as a drawn primary and glutes as secondary, from the claims named. A proposal for the LIB data card.

notes: Shared card: selector-pin.json (appliesTo lists pallof_press) covers setting the weight on the stack. No line is copied here; the sheet links the shared steps.
Stance width: ACE, StrengthLog and Motra say hip-width (c1, c2); Garage Gym Reviews says shoulder-width. The card shows hip-width.

Orientation words: ACE puts the pulley directly to one side, StrengthLog says side facing the machine, Motra says perpendicular to it, and Garage Gym Reviews says parallel to it; all describe standing side-on with the cable across the front of the chest (c1).
Hands: ACE laces the fingers around one handle (c3); BarBend squeezes the hands together and straightens the fingers on a band, which the cable handle does not need. The card draws ACE's grip.
No stop line: no read source gives a stop-for-pain line for this exercise. The low back row uses LR-6 shape (place, the source's fault, its fix) and links the back box.

Not used: Garage Gym Reviews' Pallof Press Hold and the half-kneeling, double-kneeling and overhead-reach variations are other exercises; BarBend's standing too close or too far is a set-up choice (LR-31), and its band-thickness and stack-weight lines are load choices.
